paragraphs.text: This was much in David’s mouth, as Deo gratias was in Austin’s. See Psa 103:1; Psa 103:22, after which this psalm is fitly set. There he blesseth God for his benefits to himself and the whole Church; here, for his works of creation and government common to the whole world. The Greek and Latin translations prefix this title, David de generatione Mundi. υπερ του κοσμου συστασεως, Continet opera Bereshith, saith Kimchi. It is of the same subject with the first chapter of Genesis, the first five days’ works are here after a sort considered and celebrated, as a mirror wherein God’s majesty may be clearly discerned. This psalm is by some called David’s natural theology.
paragraphs.anchor: Bless the Lord, O my soul

paragraphs.text: Non molis dimensione, sed virtutis et rerum gestarum gloria, Thou hast made thee a great name by thy works of wonder.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art very great

paragraphs.text: i.e. With thy creatures, which are as a garment, both to hide thee in one respect, and to hold thee forth in another, to be seen.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art clothed with honour and majesty

paragraphs.text: That lovely creature that first shone out of darkness, and is chief among all things sensible, as coming nearest to the unapproachable glory of God; like as the robe royal is next unto the king. Herod upon a set day came forth arrayed in royal apparel, in cloth of silver, saith Josephus, which being beaten upon by the sun’s beams, dazzled the eyes of the people, and drew from them that blasphemous acclamation, Act 12:21. God, when he made the world, showed himself in all his royalty; neither can we ascribe too much unto him.
paragraphs.anchor: Who coverest thyself with light

paragraphs.text: The whole expanse or firmament is as a canopy over God’s throne, or rather as a curtain or screen between us and the Divine majesty, the sight whereof we cannot bear.
paragraphs.anchor: Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain

paragraphs.text: God, as he hath founded the solid earth upon the fluid waters, Psa 26:9; so the highest heaven upon those waters above the firmament, Gen 1:7 Psa 17:11. This notably sets forth the wisdom and power of this Almighty architect, since artists say, In solido extruendam, The foundation of a building should be hard and rocky, and experience sealeth to it.
paragraphs.anchor: Who layest the beams of his chambers in the waters

paragraphs.text: These are his chariot royal, drawn (or rather driven) by the winds, as his chariot horses.
paragraphs.anchor: Who maketh the clouds, &c.

paragraphs.text: Immaterial substances, fit to attend upon the Father of spirits, and with speed to move suddenly and invisibly into most remote parts.
paragraphs.anchor: Who maketh his angels spirits

paragraphs.text: Seraphims they are called for their burning zeal, like so many heavenly salamanders; as also for their irresistible power; the angel that destroyed Sennacherib’s army is held to have done it by burning them within, although it appeared not outwardly, as some have been burnt by lightning.
paragraphs.anchor: His ministers a flaming fire

paragraphs.text: Heb. He hath founded the earth upon her bases. See Psa 24:2 Job 38:4; Job 38:6. {See Trapp on "Psa 24:2"} {See Trapp on "Job 38:4"} {See Trapp on "Job 38:6"}
paragraphs.anchor: Who laid the foundations of the earth

paragraphs.text: Neither can it be, by reason of its own weightiness whereby it remaineth immovable in the centre of the universe. Say it should move any way, it must move towards heaven, and so ascend, which is utterly against the nature of heavy bodies.
paragraphs.anchor: That it should not be removed for ever

paragraphs.text: Operueras, Thou hadst at first covered it, till thou for man’s sake hadst made a distinction; for else such a garment would this have been to the earth as the shirt made for the murdering of Agamemnon, where he had no issue out.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou coverest it with the deep as with a garment

paragraphs.text: As the garment, in the proper use of it, is above the body; and so they would still, did not God, for our sakes, set them their bounds and borders.
paragraphs.anchor: The waters stood above the mountains

paragraphs.text: At thy word of command and angry countenance, overawing that raging and ranging creature: so Christ rebuked the winds and waves.
paragraphs.anchor: At thy rebuke they fled

paragraphs.text: They ran away headlong, as for life.
paragraphs.anchor: They hasted away

paragraphs.text: They run any way, in post haste, breaking through thick and thin, and nowhere resting, till embodied in the abyss, their elemental place and station. This is check to our dulness and disobedience. If a man had been present, saith one, when God thus commanded the seas to retreat from the earth, he might have seen both a terrible and a joyful spectacle.
paragraphs.anchor: They go up by the mountains

paragraphs.text: A certain compass and course; an argument of God’s singular and sweet power and providence. See Job 38:10-11, {See Trapp on "Job 38:10"} {See Trapp on "Job 38:11"}
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast set a bound, &c.

paragraphs.text: God doth this; he by certain issues or vents sendeth forth the waves of the sea (which here and there break out in springs, leaving their saltness behind them), that men and other earthly creatures might have that υδωρ μεν αριστον (as Pindarus styleth it), for the satisfying of their thirst and for other necessary uses. This is David’s philosophy, and his son Solomon saith the same, Ecc 1:7; though Aristotle assign another cause of the perennity of the fountains and rivers.
paragraphs.anchor: He sendeth the springs into the valleys

paragraphs.text: A great mercy, as we have lately found in these late dry years, 1653, 1654, wherein God hath given us to know the worth of water by the want of it, Bona sunt a tergo formosissima.
paragraphs.anchor: They give drink to every beast

paragraphs.text: Those hottest creatures, Job 39:8-11.
paragraphs.anchor: The wild asses

paragraphs.text: Assuetae ripis volucres, et fluminis alveo (Virg.).
Most melodiously, many of them; therefore it is reckoned as a judgment to lose them, Jer 4:25; Jer 9:10.
paragraphs.anchor: Which sing among the branches

paragraphs.text: That is from his clouds, he giveth water to hills and high places, where wells and rivers are not.
paragraphs.anchor: He watereth the hills from his chambers

paragraphs.text: i.e. With the rain of thy clouds, dropping fatness.
paragraphs.anchor: The earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works

paragraphs.text: He caused it to grow at first, before cattle were created, Gen 1:11-12. And so he doth still, as the first cause; by rain and dew from heaven, as the second cause.
paragraphs.anchor: He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle

paragraphs.text: Ad esum et ad usum, for food, medicine, &c., Gen 1:29. Green herbs, it seemeth, was a great dish with the ancients, which, therefore, they called Holus, ab ολον. Aristippus told his fellow philosopher, who fed upon them, If you can please Dionysius you need not eat green herbs, he presently replied, If you can eat green herbs you need not please Dionysius, and be his parasite.
paragraphs.anchor: And herb for the service of man

paragraphs.text: Alma parens Tellus "Labour not for the meat that perisheth, but for the meat," &c., Joh 6:27.
paragraphs.anchor: That he may bring forth food out of the earth

paragraphs.text: That he may the more cheerfully serve his Maker, his heart being lifted up, as Jehoshaphat’s was, in the ways of obedience, Jdg 9:13 Pro 31:6-7.
paragraphs.anchor: And wine that maketh glad

paragraphs.text: The word signifieth ointments of all sorts, whereof see Pliny, lib. 12, 13. These man might want and subsist; but God is bountiful.
paragraphs.anchor: And oil to make his face to shine

paragraphs.text: In nature, Animantis cuiusque vita est fuga; were it not for the repair of nutrition the natural life would be extinguished. The Latins call bread panis, of the Greek παν; because it is the chief nourishment.
paragraphs.anchor: And bread which strengtheneth, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb. are satisfied, viz. with moisture, sucked by their roots out of the earth plentifully watered, whereby they are nourished, grow mightily, and serve man for meat, drink, medicine, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: The trees of the Lord are fall of sap

paragraphs.text: These are instanced, as tallest and most durable. God’s temple at Jerusalem was built of them; and so was the devil’s temple at Ephesus, for he will needs be God’s ape.
paragraphs.anchor: The cedars of Lebanon

paragraphs.text: Each, according to their natural instinct, with wonderful art.
paragraphs.anchor: Where the birds make their nests

paragraphs.text: That Pietaticultrix, as Petronius calleth her (and her name in Hebrew soundeth as much), because she nourisheth and cherisheth the old ones whereof she came; whence αντιπελαργειν, Genetricum senectam invicem educant (Plin.). Ciconiis pietas eximia inest (Solin.).
paragraphs.anchor: As for the stork

paragraphs.text: These wild, but weak, creatures are so wise, as to secure themselves from violence; when pursued they run to their refuges; and should not we to God, for the securing of our comforts, and safeguarding of our persons?
paragraphs.anchor: The high hills are a refuge

paragraphs.text: Most nations reckoned the year by the moon, rather than by the sun.
paragraphs.anchor: He appointed the moon for seasons

paragraphs.text: As if he were a living and intelligent creature; so justly doth he observe the law laid upon him by God, and runs through his work. See Job 38:12.
paragraphs.anchor: The sun knoweth his going down

paragraphs.text: Which, though it be dreadful, yet is it useful, and in the vicissitude of light and darkness much of God’s wisdom and goodness is to be seen. We must see that we turn not the day into night, nor night into day, without some special and urgent occasion.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou makest darkness

paragraphs.text: Rousing themselves out of their dens by night, and then usually seizing upon what prey God sendeth them in; for they are at his, and not at their own, finding.
paragraphs.anchor: The young lions roar

paragraphs.text: Like as the young ravens cry to him, Psa 147:9. by implication only. See Joe 1:18; Joe 1:20.
paragraphs.anchor: And seek

paragraphs.text: viz. Into their dens and lurking holes, smitten with fear of light and of men. A sweet providence, but little considered.
paragraphs.anchor: They yather themselves toyether

paragraphs.text: His honest employment in his particular place and calling, whether manual or mental; eating his bread in the sweat either of his brow or of his brain.
paragraphs.anchor: Man goeth forth unto his work

paragraphs.text: That time of rest and refreshment. The Lord Burleigh (William Cecil), when he put off his gown at night, used to say, Lie there, Lord Treasurer; and, bidding adieu to all state affairs, disposed himself to his quiet rest.
paragraphs.anchor: Until the evening

paragraphs.text: q.d. They are so many and so great that I cannot recount or reckon them up, but am even swallowed up of wonderment; all that I can say is, that they are magna et mirifica. In man’s body only there are miracles enough, between head and foot, to fill a volume.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord, how manifold, &c.

paragraphs.text: It is God’s great purse, Psa 24:1.
paragraphs.anchor: The earth is full

paragraphs.text: Latum manibus, id est sinubus; yet not so great and wide as man’s heart, wherein is not only that leviathan, some special foul lusts, but creeping things innumerable, crawling bugs and baggage vermin.
paragraphs.anchor: So is this great and wide sea

paragraphs.text: Far more, and of more kinds, than there are on earth.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherein are creeping things innumerable

paragraphs.text: The use whereof was first showed by God in Noah’s ark, whence afterwards Audax Iapeti genus, Japhet’s offspring sailed, and replenished the islands.
paragraphs.anchor: There go the ships

paragraphs.text: Whereof see Job 41:1-34, with notes.
paragraphs.anchor: There is that leviathan

paragraphs.text: The great housekeeper of the world, who carvest them out their meet measures of meat, and at fit seasons. Of thee they have it, per causarum concatenationem.
paragraphs.anchor: These wait all upon thee

paragraphs.text: Neither have they the least morsel of meat but what thou castest them by thy providence. Turcicure imperium quantum quantum est nihil est nisi panis mica quam dives paterfamilias proiecit caniubs, saith Luther.
paragraphs.anchor: That thou givest them they gather

paragraphs.text: By opening the bosom of the earth thou richly providest for them, ο δοτηρ εαων.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou openest thine hand

paragraphs.text: i.e. Thou withdrawest thy favour, thy concurrence, thine influence, they are troubled, or terrified, a cold sweat sitteth upon their limbs, animam agunt, they shortly expire; for in God we live, move, and have our being, Act 17:28 A frown of Augustus Caesar proved to be the death of Cornelius Gallus. Sir Christopher Hatton, Lord Chancellor of England, died Sept. 20, 1591, of a flux of his urine and grief of mind conceived upon some angry words given him by Queen Elizabeth (Camden).
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hidest thy face

paragraphs.text: Heb. Thou gatherest it, callest for it again, viz. their vital vigour.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou takest away their breath

paragraphs.text: Virtutem vivificam.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou sendest forth thy spirit

paragraphs.text: Others of the same kind are; and so the face of the earth is renewed, while another generation springeth up. This is matter of praise to their Maker.
paragraphs.anchor: They are created

paragraphs.text: Or, Let glory be to the Lord for ever, sc. for his great works of creation and conservation.
paragraphs.anchor: The glory of the Lord shall endure for ever

paragraphs.text: As he did at the creation, when he saw all to be good, and very good; so still, it doth God good, as it were, to see the poor creatures feed, and men to give him the honour of all.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord shall rejoice in his works

paragraphs.text: This must be considered, that God may be as well feared as loved and praised.
paragraphs.anchor: He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth

paragraphs.text: It is, therefore, ill falling into his hands, who can do such terrible things with his looks and touches.
paragraphs.anchor: He toucheth the hills, and they smoke

paragraphs.text: Though others be slack to do God this right, to help him to his own, to give him the glory due to his name, yet I will do it, and do it constantly, so long as I have a breath to draw.
paragraphs.anchor: I will siny unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: Or, Let it be sweet unto him, let him kindly accept it, though it be mean and worthless, through Christ’s odour poured thereinto.
paragraphs.anchor: My meditation of him shall be sweet

paragraphs.text: Withdrawing my heart from other vile and vain delights, or, at least, vexed at mine own dullness, for being no more affected with such inexplicable ravishments.
paragraphs.anchor: I will be glad in the Lord

paragraphs.text: Such sinners against their own souls, as when they know God, or might know him by his wonderful works, glorify him not as God, neither are thankful, Rom 1:21; but pollute and abuse his good creatures, to his dishonour, fighting against him with those lives that he hath given them.
paragraphs.anchor: Let the sinners be consumed, &c.

paragraphs.text: The worse others are the better be thou, kindling thyself from their coldness, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Bless thou the Lord, O my soul
